title: Causal Inference for linguistics
text:
Collider: simulate

# Adapted from https://solomon.quarto.pub/sr2/06.html#overthinking-simulated-science-distortion.
# Example from McElreath *Statistical Rethinking* (2nd ed).

set.seed(1914)

n <- 200  # Number of grant proposals
p <- 0.1  # Proportion to select

# Uncorrelated newsworthiness and trustworthiness
coll <- tibble(
  newsworthiness = rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1),
  trustworthiness = rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
) |> 
  # total_score
  mutate(total_score = newsworthiness + trustworthiness) |> 
  # Select top 10% of combined scores
  mutate(selected = ifelse(total_score >= quantile(total_score, 1 - p), TRUE, FALSE))

text:
Conditional independences












\(P \not\!\perp\!\!\!\perp C\)
\(S \not\!\perp\!\!\!\perp C\)
\(S \not\!\perp\!\!\!\perp P\)

\(\perp\!\!\!\perp\) = “independent”
\(\not\!\perp\!\!\!\perp\) = “not independent”




C = multicultural context, P = proficiency, S = code-switching. Schächinger Tenés et al. (2023)

title: Causal Inference for linguistics
text:
Conditional independences












\(P \not\!\perp\!\!\!\perp C\)
\(S \not\!\perp\!\!\!\perp C\)
\(S \not\!\perp\!\!\!\perp P | C\)

P is independent of C
S is independent of C
S is independent of P, conditional on C




C = multicultural context, P = proficiency, S = code-switching. Schächinger Tenés et al. (2023)

title: Causal Inference for linguistics
text:
Shutting the backdoor



Backdoor recipe



List all of the paths connecting X (the potential cause of interest) and Y (the outcome).
Classify each path by whether it is open or closed. A path is open unless it contains a collider.
Classify each path by whether it is a backdoor path. A backdoor path has an arrow entering X.
If there are any open backdoor paths, decide which variable(s) to condition on to close it (if possible).

title: Causal Inference: correlation is causation
text:
This is the website of the STeW workshop Causal inference: correlation is causation.







Level
🟠 Intermediate


Description
In this workshop, you will learn the basics of causal inference and how regression models can help estimate causal effects. Causal inference is based on the theory of Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), which will be introduced with examples from linguistics.


Prerequisites
Familiarity with regression models is necessary to understand the application of DAG theory to data analysis, but anyone with at least some prior statistical background is welcome to join.
